findings.title: Redis value type change from SET to ZSET on the same key prefix breaks in-flight segments
findings.body: `span-buf:s:{project:trace}:span_id` keys are switched from plain Redis SETs (`sadd`/`sscan`/`sunionstore`/`scard`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zscan`/`zunionstore`/`zcard`) while keeping the exact same key names. Keys written by the previous code version live for `redis_ttl` (default 3600s), and during a rolling deploy old and new consumers write to the same keys. Any `ZADD`/`ZCARD`/`ZUNIONSTORE`/`ZSCAN` against a key that is still a SET returns `WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value`, which raises out of the pipeline in `process_spans`/`_load_segment_data` and will crash-loop the consumer (or permanently fail those batches) until every legacy key expires. The key prefix needs to be versioned (e.g. `span-buf:z:`) or the data explicitly migrated/flushed as part of the rollout.

findings.title: zunionstore uses default SUM aggregation, corrupting span scores on duplicate payloads
findings.body: `zunionstore set_key 2 set_key span_key` (and the same call for `parent_key` on line 53) uses Redis' default `AGGREGATE SUM`. If the identical span payload is a member of both source sorted sets — which happens with at-least-once Kafka redelivery where the same payload was first buffered under the parent key and later under the redirect-resolved set key — the resulting score becomes the sum of the two `end_timestamp_precise` values (~2x epoch seconds). That span then sorts as the "newest" member forever, so the new `zpopmin` eviction will evict legitimate recent spans instead, and the score is no longer a meaningful timestamp. Use `AGGREGATE MAX` (or MIN) explicitly.

findings.title: Eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans with no metric or log
findings.body: The new trimming logic hardcodes `span_count > 1000` / `zpopmin set_key span_count - 1000`, while `SpansBuffer.__init__` still exposes `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) which is now never used, so the limit is neither configurable nor consistent with the Python config. In addition, the previous behaviour emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and an error log when a segment exceeded the span count; now spans are dropped silently inside Lua, so there is no metric, log, or dashboard signal that data loss occurred. Please make the limit a script argument driven by `max_segment_spans` and return/emit an eviction count so the loss is observable.

findings.title: Redirect-resolution loop limit silently lowered from 10000 to 1000 and its warning comment deleted
findings.body: The loop bound was changed from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the comment explaining the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was removed. This 10x reduction means segment trees deeper than ~1000 redirects now stop resolving and get split into separate segments, which is a user-visible behaviour change unrelated to the stated purpose of this PR (insert-time eviction). Either keep the previous bound or document the new limit and the reason for lowering it.

findings.title: Negative-offset slicing raises ValueError on Django querysets (comment is wrong)
findings.body: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the advanced branch passes a negative `start_offset` into `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django's `QuerySet.__getitem__` explicitly raises `ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported.")` for negative slice starts/stops before any result cache is consulted, so this path cannot work: a client supplying a cursor with a negative offset (e.g. `?cursor=0:-5:0&optimized_pagination=true`) gets an unhandled 500 instead of a 400. The in-code comment claiming "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is false, and the sibling comment "enables access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" describes behaviour that paginators elsewhere in this file deliberately reject with `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`. Negative offsets should be rejected, not forwarded.

findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator uses integer key semantics but is wired to a datetime-ordered queryset
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns `cursor.value` unchanged — these are the integer `Paginator` semantics. The only caller (`OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint`) uses it with `order_by="-datetime"`. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` that returns at least one row 500s inside `build_cursor`. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` would hand a raw integer to the `WHERE "datetime" <= %s` clause built in `build_queryset`, comparing a timestamp column against an integer and producing a database error. For a datetime-ordered queryset this class must derive from/replicate `DateTimePaginator`'s key conversion.

findings.title: organization_context.member can be None, causing an AttributeError 500
findings.body: `enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member`, which is `RpcOrganizationMember | None` and is `None` for requesters who are not org members (e.g. org auth token / integration token authenticated requests, or staff access without membership). Because `request.user.is_superuser` is `False` for those requests, the `or` does not short-circuit and the endpoint raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'has_global_access'`, turning a previously working audit-log request into a 500.

findings.title: Superuser check uses request.user.is_superuser instead of is_active_superuser(request)
findings.body: The gate for the new pagination mode uses the raw `request.user.is_superuser` flag. In Sentry, holding the superuser flag is not the same as having an elevated/active superuser session; the supported check is `sentry.auth.superuser.is_active_superuser(request)` (or staff equivalent). Using the raw flag grants the privileged code path to any account with the flag set regardless of whether superuser mode was activated, bypassing the elevation requirement that the rest of the codebase enforces. Note also that `has_global_access` is true for every member of an open-membership organization, so the "authorized administrators" framing in the comment does not match what is actually checked.

findings.title: BasePaginator now silently clamps negative forward offsets instead of failing
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` changes behaviour for every endpoint using `BasePaginator`: a forward cursor with a negative offset, which previously surfaced as an error, now silently returns the first page while `build_cursor` still derives the next/prev cursors from the original negative `cursor.offset`, producing inconsistent pagination links. Negative offsets for `is_prev` cursors are still forwarded into the slice and will raise `ValueError` from Django. This unrelated change to a widely used base class should either validate and reject negative offsets (as `OffsetPaginator` does with `BadPaginationError`) or be dropped from this PR.

findings.title: Comment claims negative cursor offsets are a supported feature, which they are not
findings.body: The added comment on `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization" for "efficient reverse pagination". Nothing in `Cursor` was changed, and the rest of the codebase explicitly rejects negative offsets (`OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`, `CallbackPaginator` all raise `BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`) while Django querysets raise `ValueError` on negative slices. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a validated, supported input.

findings.title: max_segment_spans config is now dead code
findings.body: `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` is still set in `SpansBuffer.__init__` (default 1001) but the only consumer of it — the span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` — was deleted, and the new limit is hardcoded as `1000` in `add-buffer.lua`. Anyone tuning `max_segment_spans` will silently have no effect. Either thread the value into the Lua script as an ARGV or remove the constructor parameter.

findings.title: Module docstring still describes plain sets and omits insert-time eviction
findings.body: The module docstring (steps 2-3 around line 38-39 and the glossary entry on line 58: "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still describes the span buffers as Redis sets and says the payload is added "to the set". They are now sorted sets scored by `end_timestamp_precise`, and spans are evicted (oldest-first) once a segment exceeds 1000 spans. Since this docstring is the primary explanation of the buffer's Redis layout, it should document the new type and the lossy eviction behaviour.

findings.title: Unguarded access to end_timestamp_precise can hard-fail a whole batch
findings.body: `end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"]` uses direct indexing while neighbouring optional fields use `val.get(...)`. Any message lacking the field (older producers, replayed/spillover topics, malformed payloads) raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the entire arroyo batch rather than a single message and will crash-loop the consumer on a poison message. Consider defaulting (e.g. to the message timestamp) or explicitly invalidating the single span.

findings.title: No test for the new insert-time eviction, the headline change of this PR
findings.body: All changes to `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py` are mechanical additions of `end_timestamp_precise=1700000000.0`. Nothing exercises the new behaviour: no test pushes more than 1000 spans into a segment to verify that `zpopmin` trims to the limit, that the lowest-`end_timestamp_precise` spans are the ones evicted, that the root/segment span survives, or that merging two over-limit sub-segments via `zunionstore` still trims correctly. The eviction path (and the score-based ordering it depends on) is therefore completely untested.

findings.title: New OptimizedCursorPaginator and the audit-log code path have no tests
findings.body: `OptimizedCursorPaginator` (~90 new lines, including a dedicated negative-offset branch) and the new `optimized_pagination=true` branch in `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` ship with no tests at all. Basic coverage would have caught that `get_item_key` cannot handle the `datetime` field the endpoint orders by and that negative slice starts raise `ValueError` in Django. At minimum there should be tests for: the paginator with the endpoint's actual order_by, the permission gate (member=None, non-superuser, non-privileged member), and the rejection of negative offsets.
